description: The CSO's permanent codes for first-person somatic experience: zones, sensation qualities, evidence kinds, the clinical extension's terms, and the classes and properties that structure a report. Codes carry no meaning and are never reused. Generated from cxso.ttl.

property.description: class, property or individual in the ontology
retired and kept so older data stays readable
the live code that replaces a retired one
the class a term belongs to
the short form used in practice, such as Zone 10 or T1

concept.definition: The root class for every entity in the Cathexis Somatic Ontology.
A single sensation report: where in the body (zone), what kind (quality), and optionally how intense (a whole number from 0 to 10). The atomic unit of somatic data.
A complete body state at a single moment. It holds zero or more data points; with none, nothing stands out may record that the person attended to their sensations and found nothing standing out.
A body state over time: an ordered series of snapshots for one person. Aggregates computed from the series are an implementation concern, not part of the ontology.
One of the four components of Friston's Markov blanket formalism (internal, external, sensory and active states). The clinical extension uses them to organize the classes that describe a person.
The person's physiological and psychological condition as experienced through interoception. What the person builds observer capacity for.
Environmental conditions influencing internal experience. What the person cannot directly control but must relate to.
The boundary where external becomes internal: the translation mechanism. Where prediction lives. The most clinically important component.
The person's repertoire of responses: actions to minimize prediction error. The intervention library as a toolkit of active states.
An area of the body where a person reports a sensation. A zone is the area a person reports, not a precise anatomical boundary; it is linked to UBERON where a corresponding structure exists.
Tension headaches, pressure, cognitive overwhelm.
Tension, pressure, furrowing; cognitive strain and worry patterns.
Strain, pressure, burning, tears; hypervigilance, crying suppression.
Clenching, grinding, tightness; RAGE suppression. Clinically informative.
Tightness, numbness, trembling; speech suppression, grief expression.
Constriction, lump; suppressed expression across multiple territories.
Tightness, vulnerability; exposure anxiety.
Tension, stiffness, bracing; protective posture.
Carrying, tension, elevation; extremely common across territories.
Tightness, pressure, racing; FEAR system activation, cardiac awareness.
Churning, butterflies, knot; core anxiety, diaphragmatic tension.
Nausea, churning, sinking; gut-brain axis, visceral distress.
Tension, numbness, dissociation; trauma-sensitive zone.
Tension, aching, bracing; protective posture, chronic guarding.
Aching, tension, weakness; structural support anxiety.
Heaviness, weakness, restlessness; reaching, holding and pushing gestures.
Tension, tingling, weakness; action readiness or suppression.
Clenching, tingling, numbness, sweating; highly expressive zone.
Tightness, restriction; mobility, procedural tension patterns.
Heaviness, tension, restlessness; flight readiness or collapse.
Weakness, instability; structural anxiety. Clinically informative.
Heaviness, restlessness, cramping; grounding connection.
Numbness, tingling, groundedness; grounding anchor zone.
Deep guarding, tension, numbness; trauma-sensitive, sexual and attachment associations.
Dizziness, unsteadiness, groundlessness; dissociative and transition states.
Racing, pounding, skipping; cardiac interoception distinct from chest wall tightness.
Constriction, catching, restriction; breath holding, autonomic regulation anchor.
Non-localizable sensations: diffuse fatigue, buzzing, heaviness. Genuinely systemic sensations that forcing localization would misrepresent.

Present but not yet localized. Therapeutically important for people who are developing interoceptive capacity. The ratio of unspecified-to-localized reports over time measures developing body awareness.
A phenomenological sensation descriptor. Somatic qualities, not emotional labels. Defined phenomenologically (what it feels like) rather than mechanistically (what causes it).
Constriction, gripping, clenching. FEAR activation, muscular bracing, suppressed expression. Most commonly reported quality across populations.
Radiating temperature increase, flushing. RAGE activation, shame response (facial heat), inflammatory processes.
Temperature decrease, chilling. Dissociative states, withdrawal, circulatory changes in freeze responses.
Compression, weight, bearing down. Overwhelm, suppressed affect, tension accumulation.
Fine electrical sensation, pins and needles. Autonomic arousal, hyperventilation, peripheral nervous system activation.
Absence of sensation, deadness, blankness. Dissociation, shutdown, protective disconnection from interoceptive signal.
Sharp, specific, localized nociception. Chronic pain territories, acute somatic distress, body-as-alarm.
Weight, density, gravitational pull. SEEKING suppression (Living in Shutdown), fatigue, depressive somatization.
Buoyancy, ease. Post-regulation shift, PLAY activation, reduced sympathetic tone.
Rhythmic beat, throbbing. Cardiovascular awareness, autonomic oscillation, activation pattern.
Emptiness, void, absence of substance. Grief (Living in Loss), existential states (Living in Existential Confrontation), identity emptiness (Living Behind a Mask).
An electrical hum or fizz. Anxiety activation, restlessness, autonomic hyperarousal.
Stomach turning, queasiness. Gut-brain axis distress, disgust, overwhelming affect, medication effects.
Deep, diffuse, persistent discomfort. Chronic tension patterns, grief somatization, sustained stress.
An inner oscillation felt through a zone, without visible movement. High activation, trauma-related activation, release of accumulated tension.
Calm absence of movement. Living in Shutdown: stillness as arrival, not absence. Living in Existential Confrontation: presence without action. A rare positive signal.
Outward-radiating warmth, spaciousness. A positive somatic signal, often during successful regulation. Distinct from Heat / Warmth, which has urgency: expansion is spacious.
Inward-pulling compression. Withdrawal, bracing, protective narrowing. Living in Disconnection, Living in Shame: pulling inward.
Untethered, drifting sensation. Living in an Unfamiliar Life: groundlessness. Living Under Siege: dissociative lightness. Distinct from Lightness, which has buoyancy: floating has no anchor.

Fine involuntary shaking, felt or seen as movement. Somatic discharge: can be regulatory (release after activation) or a sign of distress (Living Under Siege freeze-thaw, Living in Overwhelm spillover).

A distinct pattern of neurobiological organization. Not a diagnosis; describes how a person's nervous system is currently organized and what that organization feels like from the inside. In Pessoa's terms, a characteristic pattern of dynamic functional coalition formation.
High-precision threat predictions; ambiguous stimuli interpreted as dangerous.
Collapsed generative model; predictions of low return suppress approach behavior.
The model of the world with the person in it persists after the person is gone; prediction errors on absence.
Relational predictions suppressed; intimacy modeled as dangerous.
Multiple high-precision predictions competing simultaneously; regulatory capacity exceeded.
Locked threat predictions with extreme precision; inability to update despite safety.
Contradictory predictions with high precision in opposing directions.

concept.display: Living in the Body Under Strain
concept.definition: Brain's pain predictions maintained despite changed peripheral input; pain as construct.
Accurate predictions of genuine systemic threat; the stress response is appropriate.
Generative model of self under active reconstruction; predictions temporarily unreliable.
Self-model prediction of unworthiness; core identity prediction of defectiveness.
SEEKING system hijacked by a substance or behavior; reward predictions distorted.
False-self predictions maintained; authentic predictions suppressed.

concept.display: Living in a World Built for Someone Else
concept.definition: Sensory processing differences; predictions calibrated to atypical neurology.
Confrontation with predictions that cannot be resolved: mortality, meaning, freedom.
Memory systems themselves degrading; predictions increasingly unreliable. Procedural memory is the most resilient system.
A characteristic pattern of Markov blanket organization shared by related territories.
A blanket organization in which sensory translations are overactive: the boundary is too thin.
A blanket organization in which sensory signals are suppressed: the boundary is too thick.
A blanket organization in which the boundary is distorted: it is misshapen.
A blanket organization in which the boundary is ruptured: it is torn.
A blanket organization in which predictions may be accurate, or cannot be tested.
One of Panksepp's seven genetically encoded primary affect systems with distinct neural circuitry.
Dopaminergic motivation, exploration, curiosity. Suppression is a hallmark of Living in Shutdown.
Threat detection and defensive behavior. The primary driver of Living in Threat. Locked activation of this system is central to Living Under Siege.
Frustration, assertive response. Suppressed RAGE appears as jaw tension.
Separation distress, attachment. Primary system in Living in Loss. Suppressed in Living in Disconnection.
Nurturing, bonding. Suppression indicates relational territory involvement.
Social learning, joy, boundary-testing. Suppression is a sensitive clinical marker across all territories.
Sexual motivation. Relevant to Living in Disconnection, Living Under Siege, and relational territories.

An anatomical structure of the brain named by the neural layer of the HES. Each region is linked to its term in UBERON, the standard anatomy ontology, with skos:exactMatch, or skos:closeMatch where the match is not exact. The CSO does not define brain anatomy. UBERON does.
A brain region: the ventromedial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the anterior cingulate cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the hippocampus, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the thalamus, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the amygdala, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the anterior insula, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the posterior insula, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the somatosensory cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the hypothalamus, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the brainstem, including the periaqueductal gray, the nucleus of the solitary tract and the raphe nuclei, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the temporal pole, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the lateral temporal cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the parietal cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the occipital cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the primary motor and premotor cortex, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the basal ganglia, including the nucleus accumbens, caudate and putamen, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A brain region: the cerebellum, named by the neural layer of the HES.
A functional system of interacting brain regions, as described in the research the HES draws on. Networks are concepts of the theory, not anatomical structures, so the CSO defines them itself.
Self-referential processing, autobiographical memory, mind-wandering, future simulation. Active during rest. Overactive in rumination (Living in Shutdown).
Detects what matters: threat, novelty, reward, social significance. The switchboard that routes attention between internal and external processing.
Cognitive control, working memory, goal-directed behavior, strategic planning.
Body signal processing. Where the body's internal state becomes conscious felt experience.
Rapid threat detection and defensive response. Panksepp's FEAR system plus cortical monitoring.
Panksepp's SEEKING system. Dopaminergic circuits that drive exploration, engagement, and approach behavior.
Social cognition: reading faces, voices, intentions, and relational context. Models other minds and tracks social dynamics.
Consolidates experience into durable learning and contextualizes the present with the past. Active during reconsolidation and model updating.
Panksepp's PANIC/GRIEF circuitry. Processes separation distress, proximity-seeking, and the somatic weight of loss (Living in Loss, Living in Disconnection).
Panksepp's PLAY system. Social joy, spontaneity, and boundary-testing. Suppression is a cross-territory marker of chronic strain; its return marks recovery.
Motor execution, body schema, proprioception. The action network, engaged by movement-based regulation practices.
An ecological systems layer from Bronfenbrenner's developmental ecology. Used to classify external state entities by their proximity and influence type.
Immediate relationships and settings: partner, family, close friends, workplace team, home.
Interactions between microsystems: work-family conflict, school-home dynamics.
Indirect environments that affect the individual: partner's workplace stress, community resources, media.
Broad cultural and societal patterns: economic conditions, political climate, cultural norms.
Transitions and shifts over time: life transitions, historical events, developmental changes.
A therapeutic change mechanism, each engaging a distinct memory system.
Opens and updates emotional memory during the reconsolidation window (approximately 4 to 6 hours).
Builds new procedural patterns through repetition and reward.
Updates explicit beliefs and self-narratives through new information and reflection.
One of six capacities a person builds. They tend to develop in this order, and each earlier capacity supports the ones after it, but people move between levels and may work on several at once.
The person notices body signals with increasing precision.
The person shifts their own physiological state through practice.
The person recognizes their predictions as predictions.
The person tests predictions through action in daily life.
New experience consolidates into an updated self-model.
The person continues on their own and recognizes early warning signs.
A level of pattern detection over somatic data, from reflecting back what the person reported to predicting what comes next.
Pattern detection over internal states only.
Pattern detection over internal and external states.
Pattern detection over internal, external and sensory states.
Pattern detection over the full blanket, over time.
A type of therapeutic intervention mechanism with defined neurobiological action.
Shifts autonomic state via parasympathetic or sympathetic modulation.
Builds precision of body signal detection (anterior insular cortex).
Titrated contact with somatic activation patterns; controlled nervous system processing.
Creates controlled mismatch between prediction and experience.
Graduated contact with avoided body sensations.
Body awareness in interpersonal context.
The primary Markov blanket component this entity belongs to.
The characteristic blanket organization pattern for a territory.
Territories for which a brain region carries the strongest clinical signal.
Primary affect systems associated with a brain region.
The anatomical zone where a sensation was reported.
The phenomenological sensation quality reported.
The primary therapeutic change mechanism for a territory.
A mechanism type that serves a specific territory.
A brain network that includes a specific brain region.

An optional whole-number rating of how intense a sensation is, from 0 (not noticeable) to 10 (the most intense the person can imagine). Used on a data point, and optionally on a snapshot for the body state as a whole.
Whether this brain region is a Pessoa rich club hub with dense cross-network connectivity.
The neuroanatomical name of a brain region.
The number of a zone, from 1 to 29, as used in clinical practice ("Zone 10").
The number of a territory, from 1 to 16, as used in clinical practice ("T1").
The characteristic Panksepp affect system configuration for a territory.
The brain structures in which an affect system's circuitry lies.
The memory system a change mechanism engages.
The direction of therapeutic work for a blanket configuration.
How a data point was obtained: said by the person, measured by an instrument, sensed by a device, done in an intervention, or noticed by the system.
The person attended to their sensations and found nothing standing out. This is a report, distinct from the Numbness quality (a felt absence of sensation) and from a snapshot never taken.
The time of a somatic snapshot.
The kind of evidence by which a data point was obtained.
Obtained as something said by the person.
Obtained as a measurement by an instrument.
Obtained as something sensed by a device.
Obtained as something done in an intervention.
Obtained as something noticed by the system.
A practice type names what the person does in an intervention.
One of the ten layers of the Human Experience System (somatic, predictive, affective, neural, memory, relational, ecological, generational, technological, temporal).
A mechanism of suicide risk, following HEF Chapter 25. The ontology names the mechanisms and defines no thresholds or scores, which remain clinical and implementation decisions.
Whether a territory is currently organizing the person's experience (active) or holds installed predictions that are not currently active (dormant).
An expectation recorded before a period of experience.
A record of what happened, made after the period a prediction described.
The difference between a prediction and a later check.
The practice type of an intervention: what the person does.
The Human Experience System layer in which a data point occurred.
Associates a record with one of the four risk mechanisms.
Whether a territory is active or dormant for a person.
Breath-based regulation; exhale-dominant patterns support parasympathetic activity.
Attention moved through the body, building interoceptive awareness and observer capacity.
Attention anchored in present external sensory input.
Alternating left-right stimulation, such as tapping.
Cycles of tension and release that build awareness of the difference between them.
Practices that build a felt sense of boundary and limit how much is held at once.
Learning how predictions shape experience and how sensations are constructed; supports model updating.

Small movements and contact that raise arousal a little, for states of shutdown, heaviness or flatness (for example Living in Shutdown and Living in Shame), where regulation needs to move upward rather than toward calm.
The somatic layer of the Human Experience System.
The predictive layer of the Human Experience System.
The affective layer of the Human Experience System.
The neural layer of the Human Experience System.
The memory layer of the Human Experience System.
The relational layer of the Human Experience System.
The ecological layer of the Human Experience System.
The generational layer of the Human Experience System.
The technological layer of the Human Experience System.
The temporal dimension of the Human Experience System, the tenth of its layers.
A reason for ending that is specific to the territory, for example "there's no point" in Living in Shutdown or "I'm the problem" in Living in Shame.

The biological barrier lowering, so the person is less prevented rather than more motivated; for example metabolic conservation in Living in Shutdown, alcohol in Living in Addiction and Compulsion, dissociation in Living Under Siege.
For example intoxication in Living in Addiction and Compulsion, impulsivity in Living in Overwhelm, or means available in the environment.
The absence of a co-regulating other; for example withdrawal in Living in Disconnection, or the intact mask in Living Behind a Mask that makes a person appear fine.
Currently organizing the person's experience.
Installed predictions not currently active, which a later trigger may activate.
A data point that is part of a snapshot. A snapshot with nothing stands out set to true has none.
A snapshot that is part of a trajectory. A trajectory's snapshots are ordered by their timestamps.
